research_text:
## Research brief — `java.security.MessageDigest` / `UnsafeAlgorithm`

### 1. Governed API and meaning of the reported value

`java.security.MessageDigest` is the Java Cryptography Architecture (JCA) engine class for calculating a message digest: arbitrary-length input is processed into a fixed-length hash value. The documented lifecycle is: acquire an implementation with `getInstance`, provide input through `update` calls (or through the `digest(byte[])` convenience overload), then finalize with `digest`; finalization resets the object. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))

For this finding type, the relevant API value is the **algorithm-name string supplied when acquiring the digest implementation**—i.e., the `algorithm` argument of `MessageDigest.getInstance(String)` or a two-argument `getInstance` overload. It is **not** a value returned by `digest`, an input supplied to `update`, or the result of `isEqual`. Oracle documents the first argument to `getInstance` as “the name of the algorithm requested,” and the returned object implements that requested algorithm. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))

The supplied CrySL source binds the `algorithm` object to the first argument of its two modeled `getInstance` calls and tests it against an allow-list. Therefore, a message saying it found `SHA-1` means that the relevant constrained value is the selected factory algorithm name and that `SHA-1` is outside the rule file’s literal three-name allow-list. The rule itself does not classify the purpose of the digest—for example, whether it represents a persisted identifier, an external protocol value, a cache key, or a collision-resistant security use. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

### 2. Documented API use, security guidance, and “remediation”

**JDK API semantics.** The Java SE API documents the following usage points:

* Obtain an implementation using a standard algorithm name. With no provider argument, `getInstance` searches registered providers; it throws `NoSuchAlgorithmException` if none supports the requested algorithm. A provider-specific overload selects that provider’s implementation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))
* Feed data using `update`; call `digest()` to complete the computation. `digest(byte[])` is explicitly documented as a final `update(input)` followed by `digest()`. A `digest` call resets the object. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))
* `isEqual(byte[], byte[])` is documented as a digest equality operation; the implementation note describes its byte-examination/timing behavior. That documentation does **not** state that an equality comparison establishes authentication, integrity, or a particular security protocol role. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))
* The Java Security Standard Algorithm Names specification lists `SHA-1`, `SHA-256`, `SHA-384`, and `SHA-512` as MessageDigest names and states that standard names are case-insensitive. It lists the hyphenated spelling `SHA-256`; it does **not** list `SHA256` as a standard MessageDigest name. A provider can support additional names or aliases, but that is provider-specific. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

**What the official Java sources do not say.** The `MessageDigest` API does not deprecate `SHA-1`, label a `SHA-1` factory request as an API error, prescribe changing it to a particular alternative, or provide a persisted-data/protocol migration procedure. In fact, the current Java SE 26 API still lists `SHA-1`, `SHA-256`, and `SHA-384` as required `MessageDigest` algorithms for every Java platform implementation. That portability requirement is expressly not a security-strength assessment. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))

**Official cryptographic guidance distinct from the Java API.** NIST’s current hash-function policy says federal agencies should transition away from SHA-1 for all applications as soon as possible and use SHA-2 or SHA-3 instead; it identifies December 31, 2030 as the planned completion date for the SHA-1 transition. NIST also says SHA-2, including SHA-256/SHA-384/SHA-512, may be used for applications employing secure hash algorithms and encourages SHA-256 at minimum where interoperability is needed. This is NIST policy and transition guidance, not a Java API migration mechanism or a statement about this particular use. ([csrc.nist.gov](https://csrc.nist.gov/Projects/Hash-Functions/NIST-Policy-on-Hash-Functions))

For rule compliance specifically, the verified CrySL source accepts only its literal `SHA-256`, `SHA-384`, and `SHA-512` strings. Whether changing an existing `SHA-1` selection is appropriate depends on the unresolved use and contract: the official sources do not authorize treating a stored or externally specified SHA-1 value as interchangeable with a SHA-2 value. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

### 3. Compatibility, format, runtime support, and migration documentation

* **Digest size/output compatibility:** Java’s standard-names specification states that SHA-1 produces a 160-bit digest, SHA-256 a 256-bit digest, SHA-384 a 384-bit digest, and SHA-512 a 512-bit digest. Consequently, it is a direct technical inference that a serialized raw-digest field sized for SHA-1 differs in length from the listed SHA-2 outputs; moreover, the computed digest is algorithm-specific. The sources do **not** themselves define a wire-format or persistence compatibility rule. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

* **Persisted and wire formats:** Neither the `MessageDigest` API nor the Java standard-names specification documents an on-disk representation, wire representation, algorithm-version marker, backward-verification strategy, dual-read behavior, or rehashing/migration path for application data. That evidence must come from the relevant external format or protocol specification, not from `MessageDigest`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))

* **Platform support:** In Java SE 26, `SHA-1`, `SHA-256`, and `SHA-384` are mandatory `MessageDigest` algorithms for Java SE implementations. `SHA-512` is a standard MessageDigest name, but it is not in that mandatory three-algorithm table; the documentation says to consult implementation release documentation for additional supported algorithms. The mandatory-algorithm requirements also do not apply to third-party providers. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))

* **API-version facts:** The `MessageDigest` class is documented as present since Java 1.1; the `getInstance(String, Provider)` overload is since 1.4, and `update(ByteBuffer)` is since 1.5. Those API-introduction facts do not supply a SHA-1-to-SHA-2 migration path. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))

* **Algorithm-name compatibility:** Java specifies that standard names are case-insensitive, so capitalization variation of a listed standard name is covered. The standard name is spelled `SHA-256` with a hyphen. The documentation does not promise that removing the hyphen—for example, `SHA256`—is portable across providers. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

### 4. Exact verified `MessageDigest.crysl` rule text and scope

**Source URL:**  
`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl`

The receiver/API type declared by the source is exactly:

```text
SPEC java.security.MessageDigest
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

**Can it match a method merely because it shares a method name?** **No—not on the rule text itself.** The file declares the governed specification type as `java.security.MessageDigest`; it does not declare a global name-only rule for all methods called `getInstance`, `update`, or `digest`. The file does not, however, document the analyzer’s type-resolution implementation, subtype treatment, or any matching behavior beyond this `SPEC` declaration. Thus the source supports the type-scoped reading, but cannot by itself prove every implementation detail of a particular scanner. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

**Matched method names and parameter shapes.** The exact event clauses are:

```text
g1: getInstance(algorithm);
g2: getInstance(algorithm, _);
Get := g1 | g2;

u1: update(preInputByte);
u2: update(preInput);
u3: update(preInput, preOffset, preLen);
u4: update(preInputByteBuffer);
Update := u1 | u2 | u3 | u4;

d1: output = digest();
d2: output = digest(input);
d3: digest(output, offset, len);
DWOU := d2;
DWU := d1 | d3;
Digest := DWU | DWOU;
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

Therefore, the file **does constrain parameter-list shapes**:

* `getInstance`: one argument, or two arguments with the second represented by `_`; `algorithm` is declared `java.lang.String`. The source does not type-constrain that `_` in this clause.  
* `update`: one byte, one byte array, byte array plus two integers, or one `ByteBuffer`; the associated objects are declared respectively as `byte`, `byte[]`, `int`, and `java.nio.ByteBuffer`.  
* `digest`: no input argument with a bound return value, one input byte-array argument with a bound return value, or a three-argument output-buffer form. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

The exact ordering condition is:

```text
Get, (DWOU | (Update+, Digest))+
```

This source text permits `digest(input)` directly after `Get` (`DWOU`), and it also defines `Digest` as including all three listed digest forms after one or more `Update` events. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

The `UnsafeAlgorithm`-relevant constraint is exactly:

```text
algorithm in {"SHA-256", "SHA-384", "SHA-512"};
```

The source also contains these bounds conditions:

```text
length[preInput] >= preLen + preOffset;
preOffset >= 0;
preLen > 0;
length[output] >= len + offset;
offset >= 0;
len > 0;
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

### Source limitations and unresolved points

1. The verified rule file literally permits only the three **hyphenated** values above. The supplied detector message also includes `SHA256`, `SHA384`, and `SHA512`; that expansion is **not present in this source file**. The file alone cannot explain whether the detector normalizes aliases or used a different bundled rule revision. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))  
2. No supplied source identifies the target runtime’s Java version, providers, disabled-algorithm configuration, or whether `SHA-512` is available from the selected provider. The Java API notes provider-dependent availability. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))  
3. No supplied evidence classifies the digest’s purpose or establishes any persisted/wire/external contract. The Java and CrySL sources do not provide a migration decision for those cases.
